title: Name the subject, then the point
body: Ask: What is this about? Then: What does the writer say about it?
A topic names the subject. A main idea explains the point.
tip: Before reading the choices, finish: “This is about __, and the writer’s point is __.”

activity.evidenceText: The zoo shortened its animal signs. Children read more of them, but some adults wanted extra detail. Staff added links to longer descriptions while keeping the short signs.
activity.prompt: Which choice gives the whole point?
choices: The zoo is a place with signs.
Short signs and optional details serve readers with different needs.
activity.explanation: The short signs remain, and the links add detail. The answer needs both parts of that solution. “A place with signs” names only the subject.

workedCases.label: Another case: keep a quiet main point
workedCases.text:
Question: What is the passage mainly showing?

1. The watch no longer supplies useful time. Winding it still gives Nora a familiar ritual.
2. Combine those facts instead of choosing only “a broken watch.”

Supported answer: An old object can keep personal value after its practical use ends.

Watch for: Nothing says Nora cannot accept the loss or expects the watch to become reliable.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: Nora kept her father’s broken watch after replacing it with a reliable one. On busy mornings she no longer checked its hands, but she still wound it each Sunday. The act took less than a minute; it gave the day a familiar beginning.

title: Keep the beginning, turn, and ending
body: Look for a change: At first __. Then __. In the end __.
A good summary keeps that change. It does not stop at the first idea.
tip: Use “at first → then → finally” to keep the passage’s change in your summary.

activity.evidenceText: Kai wanted his mural to match his first sketch exactly. After neighbors described the old market, he added their memories to the design. He kept the central tree from his sketch.
activity.prompt: Which summary follows the change?
choices: Kai abandons painting after hearing criticism.
Kai replaces his whole idea with a copy of the market.
Kai keeps part of his idea while making room for neighbors’ memories.
activity.explanation: “Added their memories” shows the change; “kept the central tree” shows what remains. Neither quitting nor replacing everything matches both details.

workedCases.label: Another case: follow an argument
workedCases.text:
Question: How does the argument develop?

1. It starts with one measure of value: ticket sales.
2. It adds another measure without discarding the first.

Supported answer: The route is judged by a wider set of benefits.

Watch for: Adding a measure does not mean money stopped mattering.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The town first judged the bus route by ticket sales. A report then counted trips to jobs and clinics that had no other transport. The council kept ticket sales in its review but added access to essential services.

title: Keep the answer within the evidence
body: Check who, where, and how sure. Keep the passage’s limits.
Watch words such as all, always, and proves. They need strong support.
tip: Circle limit words in your mind: some, one group, during the trial, may, and only if.

activity.evidenceText: Eight volunteers tried the trail in dry weather. All finished comfortably. The organizer wants a rainy-day test before recommending the route to every walking group.
activity.prompt: Which summary keeps the limits?
choices: One small dry-weather trial went well; broader advice needs more evidence.
Every group can use the trail safely in any weather.
The organizer thinks the trail has no possible value.
activity.explanation: Keep eight volunteers and dry weather. A planned rainy-day test shows what is still unknown; it does not erase the useful first result.

title: Show a character’s actual change
body: Compare what the person does at the start and end.
Name only the change those actions show. One brave act does not erase every fear.
tip: Describe the final action before choosing a claim about how completely the character has changed.

activity.evidenceText: Rosa usually let her partner answer visitors’ questions. This time she explained one tool herself. She still asked her partner to handle a question she could not answer.
activity.prompt: What change is supported?
choices: Rosa no longer needs help with anything.
Rosa takes a more active role while still accepting help.
Rosa refuses to talk to visitors.
activity.explanation: Explaining one tool shows more participation. Asking for help afterward limits the change. The text does not say she has become fully independent.

title: Match the exact person or event
body: Turn the question into a small search: Who did what, and when?
Match all of those parts before choosing. A true detail can answer the wrong question.
tip: Use the question’s action as well as its name; the same person may perform several jobs.

activity.evidenceText: Luis drafted the invitation. Mei printed it, and Sam delivered it to each classroom. On Friday, Luis collected the reply slips.
activity.prompt: Who delivered the invitations?
activity.explanation: “Sam delivered it” matches the exact action. Luis drafted and collected; Mei printed. Their names are real details but answer different questions.

title: Track what happened, when, and why
body: For order, follow before, after, and the named events.
For why, find the stated reason or connect the person’s action to a nearby clue.
After alone does not prove because. Keep the explanation within the text.
tip: For “why,” connect the action to its clue; for “when,” match the event to the timeline.

activity.evidenceText: When the teacher asked for readers, Pia bent to tie a shoe that was already tied. Later, after everyone had chosen a role, she offered to carry the books.
activity.prompt: Why does Pia most likely bend toward her shoe?
choices: Her shoe needs repair before she can walk.
She wants to show the class how to tie a knot.
She is avoiding volunteering to read.
activity.explanation: The shoe is already tied, and she bends down just when readers are requested. Those linked clues support avoiding that invitation. Nothing mentions a damaged shoe or a knot lesson.

workedCases.label: Another case: separate order from cause
workedCases.text:
Question: What happens just before the crack is cleaned, and why?

1. Follow the sequence: photograph → remove handle → clean crack → reattach.
2. The text gives the reason for removal: reach the crack.

Supported answer: The handle is removed to expose the crack.

Watch for: The earlier photograph did not cause the crack, and removal was not the final step.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: First the conservator photographed the vase. She then removed its loose handle so she could reach a crack beneath it. After cleaning that crack, she reattached the handle.

title: Keep the number attached to what it counts
body: Read the noun beside the number: visits, people, items, or days.
Keep the group and time period too. Visits are not always different people.
tip: Say the unit aloud with the number: “sixty visits,” not just “sixty.”

activity.evidenceText: The clinic counted 60 appointments this week. Several patients came twice. Staff did not count how many different patients attended.
activity.prompt: What does 60 measure?
activity.explanation: The noun is appointments. Repeat visits mean one person can account for more than one appointment, so 60 is not a count of different patients.

workedCases.label: Another case: keep the changing denominator
workedCases.text:
Question: Can both descriptions be true?

1. Compare counts: 30 is more than 24.
2. Compare shares: 24/40 = 60%; 30/60 = 50%.

Supported answer: Yes: the voter count rose while the participation share fell.

Watch for: Do not carry May’s total of 40 into June’s fraction.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: In May, 24 of 40 eligible members voted. In June, 30 of 60 eligible members voted. The report calls June a larger turnout by number, while warning that a smaller share of eligible members participated.

title: Change the words, keep the meaning
body: A paraphrase says the same thing in new words.
Check the actor, action, and limit. Similar words can still change the claim.
tip: Keep “if,” “some,” and “may” when you restate a sentence; those small words change its promise.

activity.evidenceText: The principal will approve an outdoor concert if a suitable indoor room is also reserved in case of rain.
activity.prompt: Which choice keeps the condition?
choices: The principal has rejected the concert.
Approval depends on reserving an indoor backup.
activity.explanation: The indoor room is a backup condition. The sentence neither requires an indoor concert nor refuses the plan outright.

workedCases.label: Another case: keep who believes the claim
workedCases.text:
Question: What is the historian questioning?

1. Keep “authentic” separate from “firsthand.”
2. She accepts that the diary is genuine but questions its source of information.

Supported answer: Whether the diary records an eyewitness account.

Watch for: Do not turn doubt about firsthand knowledge into a claim that the diary is forged.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The historian does not deny that the diary is authentic. She questions whether its writer saw the event firsthand. A genuine document, she argues, can still repeat a rumor.

title: Build one small link from the clue
body: Use this sentence: The text says __, so __ is likely.
Stop there. Do not add a motive, event, or future success the text does not support.
tip: Finish “The text says __, so __ is likely” before accepting an inferred motive.

activity.evidenceText: Ben checked tomorrow’s train times, packed a small bag, and put his ticket beside his keys. He set his alarm for an hour before departure.
activity.prompt: What is most likely?
choices: Ben is preparing to take the train.
Ben drives the train for work.
activity.explanation: The times, ticket, bag, and alarm work together as travel preparations. None gives Ben a job on the train or shows a cancellation.

workedCases.label: Another case: connect two clues
workedCases.text:
Question: What does her final action most likely suggest?

1. The hinge repair held, but scraping returned.
2. Reaching for height notes suggests she is checking another possible source of the problem.

Supported answer: She is investigating a cause beyond the loose hinge.

Watch for: The notes do not yet prove which cause is responsible.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: A technician marked the loose hinge, then recorded the door’s height before tightening it. On her next visit, the hinge held firm but the door again scraped the floor. She reached for her height notes rather than another screw.

title: Choose what the text supports
body: “Could happen” is weaker than “this text gives a reason to expect it.”
Ask which detail supports the answer. A possible story without a clue is not enough.
tip: Ask which exact clue makes this answer likely, not just possible in real life.

activity.evidenceText: The chef tried a new soup at one lunch service. Several customers asked for it again. She planned another trial before adding it to the regular menu.
activity.prompt: What does the next trial suggest?
choices: The soup is already guaranteed a permanent place.
The chef sees enough promise to test it again.
activity.explanation: Requests for more and another trial support interest. “Before adding it” keeps the permanent decision open.

title: Read feelings from words and actions
body: Look at what the person says and does. Both are clues.
Match how strong the feeling is. A worry is not always a refusal.
tip: Keep both halves when someone praises an idea but adds a worry or condition.

activity.evidenceText: “I like the plan,” Mo said, “but I cannot help on weekdays.” He offered to join the planting team on Saturday.
activity.prompt: Which attitude fits Mo?
choices: He supports the plan with a limit on his availability.
activity.explanation: His praise and Saturday offer show support. “Cannot help on weekdays” gives the limit; it does not cancel his support.

workedCases.label: Another case: trust the action as well as the words
workedCases.text:
Question: What attitude best fits Luis before dinner?

1. His words sound confident, but keeping the bracket shows a backup plan.
2. Watching the shelf and later putting the bracket away show that his confidence develops.

Supported answer: Outward support mixed with private doubt.

Watch for: Neither total trust nor outright opposition fits both his words and actions.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: “Of course your way will work,” Luis told his sister. Still, he kept the old bracket in his coat pocket and watched the new shelf through dinner. When it stayed level, he finally put the bracket away.

title: Try to disprove the tempting answer
body: Ask: If this answer were true, what else would have to be true?
Check that claim against the passage. One clear contradiction can eliminate it.
tip: To test a strong answer, look for one action or sentence that would make it false.

activity.evidenceText: Ava complained that the first rehearsal was messy. She then made a practice schedule and returned early the next day to help set up.
activity.prompt: What best challenges “Ava gave up on the show”?
choices: She returned early and made a practice schedule.
She noticed a problem at rehearsal.
The rehearsal happened before the next day.
activity.explanation: Her later actions show continued effort. A complaint about one rehearsal does not establish that she quit the whole project.

workedCases.label: Another case: challenge a theory with new evidence
workedCases.text:
Question: What does the new result challenge?

1. “Only because the feeder remains” makes its presence necessary.
2. The birds return when it is absent, contradicting that requirement.

Supported answer: The claim that the feeder must be present.

Watch for: The result does not identify the true cause or show that food never matters.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: A researcher claims the birds return only because the old feeder remains. During one week the feeder is removed, yet marked birds return to the same place at the usual hour.

title: Make a plain-word replacement
body: Cover the choices and replace the word with a simple phrase.
Then choose the answer closest to your phrase. Read it back in the sentence.
tip: Guess a plain meaning before reading the choices, then plug that meaning back into the sentence.

activity.evidenceText: The editor called the ending abrupt. The story stopped in the middle of the argument, giving readers no warning that the last page was near.
activity.prompt: What does “abrupt” mean here?
activity.explanation: “Stopped ... giving readers no warning” points to sudden. The sentence concerns how the story ends, not a slope or someone’s manners.

title: Use the clue beside the word
body: Look for a contrast, example, or explanation nearby.
Words such as but, rather than, and unlike often show which meaning fits.
tip: Look beside “but,” “unlike,” or “rather than”; the contrast often gives you the definition.

activity.evidenceText: The vote was deferred rather than held that afternoon. Members wanted the new cost figures before making their decision.
activity.prompt: What does “deferred” mean?
activity.explanation: “Rather than held that afternoon” and waiting for figures show a delay. The passage gives no result of a completed vote.

title: Notice when a word makes a picture
body: Some words describe an idea as if it were a physical thing.
Ask what is actually changing. Keep the comparison’s meaning without taking it literally.
tip: Name what is being described before deciding whether the word is literal or a comparison.

activity.evidenceText: The missing permit acted as a brake on the project. Workers had the materials ready but could not begin until the approval arrived.
activity.prompt: What does “brake” mean here?
choices: Something that slows or stops progress
A broken part of a truck
Proof that the project is finished
activity.explanation: The permit delay prevents work from starting, like a brake slows movement. No vehicle part appears in this situation.

workedCases.label: Another case: keep a subtle comparison
workedCases.text:
Question: What does the bridge image suggest?

1. A bridge allows movement across a gap. “Thin” and the weight warning make this one fragile.
2. Together, the words describe limited progress rather than a complete solution.

Supported answer: A fragile agreement makes initial talks possible.

Watch for: The passage describes no actual bridge and does not say the dispute is fully settled.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The committee’s agreement was a thin bridge across the dispute. Both sides could use it to begin talks, but neither trusted it with the weight of a final settlement.

title: Check the word against the whole point
body: A replacement must fit both the sentence and the point around it.
Reject a meaning that fits the general topic but changes this particular claim.
tip: After substitution, reread the whole claim; a topic-related meaning can still contradict the writer.

activity.evidenceText: The first estimate was tentative. The team used it to plan supplies but expected to revise it after counting the remaining boxes.
activity.prompt: Which meaning fits “tentative”?
activity.explanation: The estimate is useful for planning but may change after another count. “Not yet final” keeps both facts; false and unrelated do not.

workedCases.label: Another case: let context choose the sense
workedCases.text:
Question: What does “exacting” mean here?

1. The final sentence explains the effect: a stricter standard.
2. A demanding standard fits both better color visibility and exposed repairs.

Supported answer: Demanding close accuracy or care.

Watch for: “Exact copy” shares part of the word but does not fit what the lighting does.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The curator called the new lighting exacting. It revealed color differences that the old lamps hid, but it also made tiny repairs stand out. Under it, the staff had to work to a stricter standard.

title: Name the paragraph’s job
body: Read the paragraph with the one before and after it.
Finish this sentence: The writer includes this to __. A job is more than a topic.
tip: For a purpose question, answer “Why put this here?” instead of repeating what the detail says.

activity.evidenceText: The writer says delivery delays affect small businesses. She describes a baker who had to cancel an order when flour arrived late. She then proposes clearer arrival notices.
activity.prompt: Why include the baker?
choices: To give a history of bread
To show a concrete effect of a delivery delay
activity.explanation: The canceled order shows a delay causing a practical problem. It supports the claim about businesses; it is not a claim about every business.

workedCases.label: Another case: an example can limit a claim
workedCases.text:
Question: What is the family’s role in the argument?

1. Place it between the praise and the recommendation.
2. The case exposes a limit in the original approach and explains why broader testing is needed.

Supported answer: To qualify the praise and support the proposed improvement.

Watch for: A limiting example need not reject labels altogether or represent every family.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The essay praises standardized library labels for making shelves easier to use. It then describes a bilingual family whose questions were absent from those labels. The final paragraph recommends testing labels with varied visitors.

title: Match the feeling and its strength
body: Tone means the writer’s attitude. Find words that show it.
Match both the feeling and how strong it is: worried is different from furious.
tip: Find two tone clues; match the strength of the feeling as well as whether it is positive.

activity.evidenceText: This guide is useful and easy to follow. I wish the maps were larger, but I would recommend it to anyone visiting the city for the first time.
activity.prompt: Which tone fits?
activity.explanation: “Useful,” “easy to follow,” and “recommend” establish approval. Wanting larger maps adds a specific criticism without reversing it.

workedCases.label: Another case: notice dry humor
workedCases.text:
Question: What tone does the last sentence create?

1. Compare the efficiency promise with the needless meetings and repeated forms.
2. The restrained wording points out that mismatch through irony.

Supported answer: Dryly skeptical about the promised efficiency.

Watch for: This is neither literal praise nor proof that Mira rejects every new system.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The new notice system was said to save everyone time. By noon, Mira had attended two meetings about it and filled out a form requesting the right form. Efficiency, she wrote in her notebook, appeared to require a patient audience.

title: Track a speaker’s view and how it changes
body: Keep each speaker’s view separate from the author’s. Check the response after a quote.
For a change in viewpoint, compare the opening view with the later one.
Name what is added, challenged, or kept. A new view may extend an old one instead of rejecting it.
tip: For a shift, finish “At first __; later __.” For a quote, read the response that follows.

activity.evidenceText: “Nobody uses that path,” the official said. The reporter watched six children use it to reach school and asked why they were missing from the official count.
activity.prompt: What does the reporter do with the official’s claim?
choices: Proves every resident uses the path
activity.explanation: Six children using the path contradict nobody. The observation challenges the quote without proving a claim about every resident.

workedCases.label: Another case: a viewpoint changes without reversing
workedCases.text:
Question: How does her view change?

1. At first she treats the problem as visitor error. Later she gathers their perspective and changes the sign.
2. The courtyard stays, so she revises the approach without rejecting the whole design.

Supported answer: She begins taking visitors’ experience into account.

Watch for: Keeping part of the design does not mean her outlook stayed unchanged.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: At first, the designer blamed visitors for missing the entrance. She watched a family circle the building twice and asked where they expected a door. She kept the design’s courtyard but moved its main sign to face the street.

title: Explain what an image helps us notice
body: For a comparison, name the feature the two things share.
Connect that feature to the scene. Do not bring in every fact about the comparison.
tip: Ask “What do these two things share here?” Keep only the feature supported by nearby words.

activity.evidenceText: From the hill, the line of bus headlights looked like a necklace of lights. Each small glow followed the next around the curve below.
activity.prompt: What feature does the necklace comparison emphasize?
choices: A linked row of small bright points
activity.explanation: The line of lights curving one after another supplies the shared feature. A necklace’s cost and use as clothing are not part of this image.

workedCases.label: Another case: follow a repeated object
workedCases.text:
Question: What does the key’s repeated appearance help show?

1. First it is a tightly held backup; later she sets it down while considering the offer.
2. Taking it back preserves caution, while the looser grip suggests greater openness.

Supported answer: Her cautious movement toward accepting a new possibility.

Watch for: The key alone does not establish a literal move, a final promise, or complete confidence.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: At the interview, Ana gripped the spare key until its teeth marked her palm. Later she placed it on the table while proposing a trial month. Before leaving, she took it back but no longer held it tightly.

title: Find the agreement and the difference
body: Ask what both writers support. Then ask what one adds or changes.
A condition such as “only if” can be the main difference.
tip: Write “A says __; B says __” before deciding whether B agrees, disagrees, or adds a condition.

activity.evidenceText:
A: “The playground should open later so more families can use it.”

B: “I support later hours if lighting is installed first. Children need to see the paths after dark.”
activity.prompt: How do their views compare?
choices: Both support later hours; B adds a lighting condition.
activity.explanation: Both support the same opening change. “If ... first” is B’s condition. A’s silence does not establish opposition to lights.

evidence.title: Same goal, added condition
evidence.context: Keep each writer’s view in its own row.

title: Keep only what both sources support
body: Check each part of the answer against its evidence.
Within one passage, compare the two named moments: what stays, changes, or connects?
Across sources, keep both claims and their limits. Do not add a cause or promise neither source establishes.
tip: For a comparison, point to evidence on both sides; name the relationship instead of listing two facts.

activity.evidenceText: The garden report says 12 families received vegetables this month. The budget note says donations paid for this month’s seeds, but next month’s funding is still unknown.
activity.prompt: Which statement uses both sources correctly?
choices: It served 12 families this month, while future seed funding remains unknown.
The garden served no families because funding is uncertain.
activity.explanation: The report supplies the family count, and the note limits the funding. This month’s result is real without a promise about later months.

workedCases.label: Another case: connect the beginning and ending
workedCases.text:
Question: Does the ending reverse the opening advice?

1. The opening concerns long storage. The ending concerns brief preparation just before planting.
2. Keep those different stages attached to the advice; the two instructions can both apply.

Supported answer: No. The advice applies at different stages.

Watch for: Dropping “during storage” or “planting immediately” creates a contradiction the article does not make.

evidence.title: Read the evidence
evidence.context: The article opens by warning gardeners to keep seeds dry during storage. Near the end, it recommends soaking certain seeds briefly before planting them immediately. It explains that long storage and preparation for planting have different goals.

title: Read the table’s labels, then compare
body: Read what each number counts. For a share, divide the part by the whole.
Then connect that result to the passage. A higher count can still be a smaller share.
tip: For a percent or share, write “part ÷ whole” before comparing two raw counts.

activity.prompt: How did the on-time return rate change?
choices: The on-time share rose because the count rose.
The reminders alone explain the result.
The count rose, but the on-time share fell from 60% to 50%.
activity.explanation: 18 ÷ 30 = 60%; 30 ÷ 60 = 50%. Count and share move differently. Changed opening hours also prevent isolating the reminders’ effect.

evidence.title: Book returns
evidence.context: The library added reminders and changed its opening hours at the same time.

evidence.title: Count and share can move differently
evidence.context: Read the column headings before comparing the two meeting counts.

workedCases.label: Another case: combine groups before taking a rate
workedCases.text:
Question: What is the combined success rate across both groups?

1. Combine successful results: 18 + 8 = 26. Combine all attempts: 20 + 40 = 60.
2. Divide once: 26/60 ≈ 43%. The larger group contributes more attempts.

Supported answer: About 43%.

Watch for: Averaging 90% and 20% gives 55%, which wrongly treats unequal group sizes as equal.

evidence.title: Two unequal groups
evidence.context: The passage reports all attempts; no attempt is in both groups.

title: Keep every source’s limits
body: Check who was measured and under which conditions.
A combined answer must keep the limits from all sources, even if a broader answer sounds useful.
tip: Check the group, setting, and measured result in every source before accepting a broad conclusion.

activity.evidenceText: A report says six volunteers preferred the new lamp. A second note says the trial lasted one evening in one room. Nobody measured reading speed.
activity.prompt: What can the sources support together?
choices: Those volunteers preferred the lamp in that brief trial.
The lamp makes everyone read faster.
The lamp has been tested in every kind of room.
activity.explanation: Keep the six volunteers, preference, and short trial. Reading speed, every person, and other rooms were not measured.

title: Find the right row or line
body: 1. Read what the question wants: a value, a change, or a rate.
2. Use the row label or bottom axis to find the condition. Pick the named column or line.
3. Read the value and its unit.

activity.prompt: A thermometer table lists elapsed time and temperature. Which column answers “how warm at 4 min”?
activity.explanation: The question asks for temperature at a specified time. Time selects the row; temperature is the requested output.

evidence.title: A new temperature record
evidence.context: Find the requested quantity after selecting the time.

evidence.title: Two seedling groups
evidence.context: Heights are measured on the same days. Solid = U; dashed = V.

tip: Say the column or line name before reading its number.

title: Amount, change, or percent?
body: 1. Final = start + change. Amount removed = start − final.
2. A fraction is part ÷ whole. For percent removed, the whole is the start; for a group’s share, use the combined total.
3. Percent = fraction × 100. Count = percent ÷ 100 × total. Percentage-point difference just subtracts percentages.

activity.prompt: A sample falls from 50 to 20 mg/L. What percentage of its initial concentration was removed?
activity.explanation: Removal is 50−20 = 30 mg/L. Divide by the initial 50, not the remaining 20: 30/50 = 60%.

evidence.title: A different sample
evidence.context: The volume stays the same.

evidence.title: Water treatment
evidence.context: The water volume stays the same.

tip: Circle “removed” or “remaining”; those words choose different numerators.

workedCases.label: Another case: choose the whole
workedCases.text:
Question: What fraction are young, and how many young would the same share give in a group of 45?

1. The whole is 12 + 18 = 30. Young share = 12 ÷ 30 = 40%.
2. Keep that share: 0.40 × 45 = 18.

Supported answer: 2/5 young; 18 in the larger group.

Watch for: 12 ÷ 18 compares young with adults; it is not the young share of everyone.

evidence.title: One group, two parts
evidence.context: Every animal is counted once. The larger group has the same young share.

workedCases.label: Another case: percentage points
workedCases.text:
Question: The share rises from 40% to 60%. How many percentage points is that?

1. Subtract the percentages: 60 − 40 = 20 points.
2. For percent increase instead, divide that 20 by the starting 40: 50%.

Supported answer: 20 percentage points.

Watch for: “Percentage points” and “percent increase” name different calculations.

evidence.title: Share before and after
evidence.context: Both numbers are percentages of their own groups.

title: Check both requirements
body: 1. Write each requirement separately.
2. Cross out a row if it fails either one. “At least” and “at most” allow equality.
3. If a requirement says “per,” divide first: insects per area = insects ÷ area.

activity.prompt: Which water sample meets BOTH temperature below 25°C and oxygen at least 6 mg/L?
activity.explanation: M has 24°C and 6 mg/L and passes both. N fails the strict temperature limit; O fails the oxygen minimum.

evidence.title: Choosing a water sample
evidence.context: Temperature must be below 25°C; oxygen must be at least 6 mg/L.

evidence.title: Choosing an air filter
evidence.context: A filter must have airflow at least 70 m³/min and dust at most 7 mg/m³.

tip: A candidate must pass every requirement, even if it wins one category.

title: Compare amounts per equal size
body: 1. Find the amount and its own sample size. For a group’s share, the whole includes all groups.
2. Divide amount ÷ size before comparing. Keep the unit: insects/L, for example.
3. For a supplied ratio, use the named numerator and denominator. Recover an amount with ratio × sample size.

activity.prompt: Which pool has the greater insect density?
activity.explanation: U has 24/3 = 8 insects/L; V has 30/6 = 5 insects/L. Dividing by volume makes the samples comparable.

evidence.title: Two insect pools
evidence.context: Density means insects per liter.

evidence.title: Two plant plots
evidence.context: The plots have different areas.

tip: “Per” tells you to divide; read which unit belongs on the bottom.

title: Read a change or a repeating period
body: 1. For a gain, subtract the starting height from the ending height.
2. For a rate, divide the gain by elapsed time.
3. For a repeating period, measure from one peak to the next peak. One event alone cannot show its repeat time.

activity.prompt: A population rises from 120 at hour 2 to 180 at hour 5. What is its average increase per hour?
activity.explanation: Use change divided by elapsed time: (180−120)/(5−2) = 60/3 = 20 organisms/h.

evidence.title: A new population
evidence.context: The graph shows the population at two times.

evidence.title: Plant height
evidence.context: Each point gives height, not growth per day.

tip: Mark both endpoints; elapsed time is their difference, not the final time.

title: Use the equation the passage gives
body: 1. Write what each letter means and circle the quantity requested.
2. Rearrange before substituting: from Q = mcΔT, temperature increase is ΔT = Q ÷ (mc).
3. Calculate the requested output for each sample. At fixed heat, doubling mass halves the temperature increase.

activity.prompt: For the supplied output P = VI, which device has greater power?
activity.explanation: D gives 4×9 = 36 mW; E gives 6×5 = 30 mW. Compare products rather than voltage alone.

evidence.title: Different devices
evidence.context: Use P = VI. Volts × milliamps gives milliwatts.

evidence.title: Same heat, different water masses
evidence.context: Use Q = mcΔT. Q is energy, m is mass, c = 4 J/(g·°C), and ΔT is temperature increase. No heat is lost.

tip: Write the requested output beside your answer so you do not stop halfway.

workedCases.label: Another case: find time
workedCases.text:
Question: How long does the charge last at the stated current?

1. From capacity = current × time, divide capacity by current.
2. 6 Ah ÷ 0.4 A = 15 h.

Supported answer: 15 hours.

Watch for: Keep the requested letter alone first; do not multiply just because two values are given.

evidence.title: A supplied rule
evidence.context: Capacity = current × time. The current stays constant.

title: Combine two streams
body: 1. For each stream, multiply concentration × water flow to get pollutant per second.
2. Add both pollutant flows and both water flows.
3. Mixed concentration = total pollutant flow ÷ total water flow.

activity.prompt: A supplies 12 L/s at 2 mg/L and B supplies 4 L/s at 10 mg/L. What concentration follows complete mixing?
activity.explanation: Mass flow is 12×2+4×10 = 64 mg/s. Water flow is 16 L/s. The flow-weighted concentration is 64/16 = 4 mg/L.

evidence.title: A different confluence
evidence.context: The solute is conserved and the streams mix completely.

evidence.title: Two streams mix
evidence.context: No pollutant is lost. Water mixes completely.

tip: The larger water flow pulls the mixed concentration closer to its own concentration.

title: Turn a sensor reading into an amount
body: 1. For a calibration graph, start at the signal and follow the correct line back to concentration. For an equation, keep its offset.
2. Undo dilution: multiply by the dilution factor.
3. Apply the new flow, then multiply concentration × flow. Compare the final amounts, or divide them if asked for a fraction.

activity.prompt: After its flow is halved, how much pollutant does Stream A carry each second?
activity.explanation: Signal 2 gives C = 3×2 = 6 mg/L in the diluted liquid; threefold dilution means original C = 18 mg/L. New flow is 1 L/s, so mass flow is 18 mg/s.

evidence.title: A new calibration
evidence.context: C = 3S mg/L. No solute is lost during dilution. Only the original flow is halved.

evidence.title: Two calibrations and a changed flow
evidence.context: Each calibration line includes its 2-unit blank signal. Read the diluted liquid’s concentration from its own line. Multiply by the dilution factor to recover the original concentration. Only A’s original flow is halved.

tip: Label intermediate values “diluted” and “original” to avoid mixing the two.

workedCases.label: Another case: follow the value through
workedCases.text:
Question: How much pollutant flows each second after flow is divided by three?

1. Diluted concentration = (10 − 1) ÷ 3 = 3 mg/L.
2. Undo dilution: 3 × 4 = 12 mg/L. New flow = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 L/s.
3. Amount per second = 12 × 2 = 24 mg/s.

Supported answer: 24 mg/s.

Watch for: Subtract the blank once. A graph that already includes the blank needs no second subtraction.

evidence.title: Signal → concentration → amount
evidence.context: Use C = (S − 1) ÷ 3. Dilution loses no pollutant; only flow changes.

title: Estimate between two points
body: 1. Find the two measured points just below and above the target.
2. Halfway across means halfway up or down. For another position, use that fraction of the change.
3. Only use a straight-line estimate when allowed. A supplied curved model takes priority.

activity.prompt: Using straight-line interpolation, estimate the temperature at 7 min.
activity.explanation: Seven minutes is halfway from 5 to 9 min, so use the midpoint of 46 and 34: (46+34)/2 = 40°C.

evidence.title: A different cooling sample
evidence.context: Use a straight line between the measured points.

evidence.title: Cooling between measurements
evidence.context: Use a straight-line estimate between these points.

tip: Bracket the target with its nearest two points before doing any arithmetic.

title: Compare how fast values change
body: 1. Subtract the two values in each interval.
2. Divide each change by its own time gap.
3. Compare the sizes of the rates. Falling values have negative rates; a smaller drop per minute means slower cooling.

activity.prompt: Which interval has the greater average cooling rate in magnitude?
choices: Neither interval, because only instantaneous rates can be compared
activity.explanation: Compare temperature change divided by interval length: the first magnitude is 16/2 = 8°C/min and the second is 18/6 = 3°C/min. The second total drop is larger, but it takes three times as long. Falling in both intervals does not make the rates equal, and average rates can be compared without instantaneous measurements.

evidence.title: Another cooling trial
evidence.context: Compare average cooling, not just total drops.

evidence.title: Cooling over unequal times
evidence.context: The sample keeps cooling, but the time gaps differ.

tip: A steeper downward line means faster cooling, not a colder final temperature.

workedCases.label: Another case: distance takes time
workedCases.text:
Question: How much longer does 6→8 mm take than 2→4 mm?

1. 2→4 mm takes 3 − 1 = 2 minutes.
2. 6→8 mm takes 15 − 8 = 7 minutes. Compare durations: 7 − 2 = 5.

Supported answer: 5 minutes longer.

Watch for: For “how much longer,” subtract times at the named distances; do not subtract the distances.

evidence.title: A moving front
evidence.context: Use the time for each named position.

title: Stay within what was measured
body: 1. For the highest tested value, compare the plotted points.
2. A value between measurements is an estimate; a value outside them is an extrapolation.
3. Do not turn “highest tested” into “highest possible” or a short trend into “always.”

activity.prompt: A response is 4, 11, and 8 at doses 1, 3, and 5. Which claim is supported?
choices: Dose 3 has the largest measured response
The true maximum must occur exactly at dose 3
Response increases throughout the interval from dose 1 to dose 5
The response at dose 4 is known to be exactly 9.5
activity.explanation: Among the three measured outputs, 11 at dose 3 is largest. The fall to 8 at dose 5 contradicts a continuously increasing claim. No measurements locate an exact overall optimum or establish a straight-line value of 9.5 at dose 4; those add claims beyond the observations.

evidence.title: Three doses
evidence.context: Only the shown doses were measured; no rule between points is supplied.

evidence.title: Temperature and activity
evidence.context: Only the three shown temperatures were tested.

tip: Check the first and last tested inputs before accepting “always” or “never.”

title: Separate starting value from rate
body: 1. In y = start + rate × x, separate the start from the rate.
2. Rate = vertical change ÷ horizontal change. Direct proportion needs both a zero start and a constant output/input ratio.
3. For an amount above a baseline or limit, subtract that baseline or limit from the total.

activity.prompt: For T = 18−3d, what is the temperature change per meter?
activity.explanation: The coefficient of d is the slope: each additional meter lowers temperature by 3°C. The 18°C intercept is the value at zero depth.

evidence.title: Temperature with depth
evidence.context: Use T = 18 − 3d. T is in °C and d is in meters.

evidence.title: Pressure at depth
evidence.context: The supplied rule is P = 90 + 12d, with d in meters and P in kPa.

tip: Read the value at input zero before calling a relationship directly proportional.

workedCases.label: Another case: direct proportion
workedCases.text:
Question: Which output is directly proportional to x?

1. P starts at zero and P/x stays 4 for positive x.
2. T starts at 5. When x doubles from 2 to 4, T goes 13→21, not 13→26.

Supported answer: P only.

Watch for: A constant slope is not enough. Direct proportion also needs a zero start.

title: Use squares and roots carefully
body: 1. If x² = kt, find k by dividing a measured x² by its matching time t.
2. Substitute the new time, then take the square root to recover distance x.
3. With fixed k, x² versus t is a straight line. Doubling x takes four times the time.

activity.prompt: For x² = 9t, what distance is predicted at 16 min?
activity.explanation: Substitute t = 16: x² = 144. The nonnegative distance is √144 = 12 mm; 144 is squared distance.

evidence.title: A new spreading model
evidence.context: Use x² = 9t; x is a nonnegative distance in mm and t is minutes.

evidence.title: A spreading front
evidence.context: The model says squared distance x² is directly proportional to time t: x² = kt. The constant k must be found from a measured point.

tip: Keep the square on the unknown until you take the square root.

workedCases.label: Another case: make the curved rule straight
workedCases.text:
Question: Which graph gives a straight line?

1. Square each distance: 2² = 4, 4² = 16, 6² = 36.
2. Squared distance ÷ time stays 4, so x² versus time is straight.

Supported answer: Squared distance against time.

Watch for: Ordinary distance against time is curved; squaring the vertical quantity changes the graph.

evidence.title: Squared distance
evidence.context: The model is x² = 4t. Distance is nonnegative.

title: Rising, flattening, or turning?
body: 1. Read each change from left to right.
2. A plateau flattens. A turning point changes from rising to falling, or falling to rising.
3. Check later measurements and the instrument’s limit before claiming the real process has stopped.

activity.prompt: Which series has a turning point rather than only slowing growth?
activity.explanation: The selected series rises to 10 and then falls to 6, so its direction reverses. Smaller positive increases alone do not create a turning point.

evidence.title: Four possible patterns
evidence.context: Each column is one equal input step.

evidence.title: Signal over equal time steps
evidence.context: The detector can read up to 100 units. These are the only measured steps.

tip: Follow the curve left to right; flattening and falling are different patterns.

title: Changed, measured, or kept the same?
body: 1. Changed on purpose = independent variable. Measured result = dependent variable.
2. Kept the same = controlled variable.
3. A control group is the comparison. To test a drug in oil, compare with the same oil without the drug.

activity.prompt: To test the active drug dissolved in oil, what should the comparison group receive?
choices: The same oil without the drug
activity.explanation: An oil-only control holds the carrier constant. Comparing against no oil changes both drug presence and carrier presence.

evidence.title: Testing a drug carried in oil
evidence.context: To test the drug alone, hold the oil amount and all other conditions fixed.

evidence.title: Fertilizer and leaves
evidence.context: Same species, water, light, and 12-day duration. Fertilizer dose is assigned to separate plants.

tip: Name the measured result in everyday words before labeling it the dependent variable.

title: Change one cause at a time
body: 1. Name the factor the study wants to test.
2. Check whether another relevant factor changes with it. That is a confound: two possible causes are mixed.
3. Keep the other factor the same. More repeats do not repair a mixed comparison.

activity.prompt: Heated pots receive more water than cool pots. Which change most directly isolates heating?
choices: Use the same water amount in both groups
Use a more precise thermometer in both groups
activity.explanation: Heating and water amount currently vary together. Giving both groups the same water isolates heating. More measurements, more heated pots, or a more precise thermometer can improve sampling or precision while leaving the water confound intact.

evidence.title: Another mixed comparison
evidence.context: All conditions except those shown are matched.

evidence.title: A temperature test with a problem
evidence.context: The investigators want to test temperature alone.

tip: List what differs between groups; a second relevant difference can explain the result.

title: Choose a fair comparison
body: 1. Name the one factor in the question.
2. Choose two groups that differ in that factor while the other conditions match.
3. Use the same measured result and time or stopping point in both groups.

activity.prompt: To test whether stirring changes dissolving time, which pair is best?
choices: Stirred hot water versus unstirred cold water
Equal masses and water temperatures; stirred versus unstirred
Stirred water with twice the solid versus unstirred water with the original solid mass
Two stirred cups at different temperatures
activity.explanation: Compare stirred and unstirred cups at the same solid mass and water temperature. Equal water volumes and a shared endpoint complete the control. Changing temperature or mass with stirring mixes causes, while two stirred cups do not test stirring at all.

evidence.title: Testing stirring
evidence.context: All cups have equal water volumes and use the same dissolving endpoint.

evidence.title: Catalyst shape
evidence.context: Use the same solution and temperature. Stop timing when 30 mL gas forms.

tip: To test a cause→effect explanation, measure its proposed middle step, not just the final result.

workedCases.label: Another case: test the middle step
workedCases.text:
Question: The model says light opens leaf pores, increasing water loss. What extra measurement tests the first step?

1. Water loss measures the final result, not whether pores opened.
2. Count open pores per equal leaf area in both matched groups.

Supported answer: Open pores per equal area in light and dark.

Watch for: Measuring only more water loss cannot show which proposed step caused it.

evidence.title: A proposed two-step cause
evidence.context: Same plant type, leaf area, temperature, humidity and duration. Only light differs.

title: Count the separately treated units
body: 1. Find what receives its own treatment: a tank, tray, animal, or sample.
2. Count those independent units, not every repeated reading inside one unit.
3. Repeats show how consistent results are. They do not remove a shared measurement bias.

activity.prompt: Three independently treated trays each contain 12 seedlings. How many experimental units received treatment independently?
activity.explanation: Treatment was assigned to trays, so the independent units are the three trays. More seedlings improve sampling within a tray but do not create more treatment assignments.

evidence.title: Seedlings in trays
evidence.context: Each entire tray receives its own treatment; seedlings are not separately assigned.

evidence.title: Fish in treated tanks
evidence.context: Salinity is assigned separately to each whole tank; fish in a tank share its water.

tip: Ask what got its own treatment assignment, not how many numbers were recorded.

title: Match the fix to the problem
body: 1. Starting-group differences: assign treatments randomly.
2. Scorer expectations: hide treatment labels (blinding).
3. Earlier exposure: use fresh groups or adequate recovery. Reverse order to check whether order matters.

activity.prompt: Which change most directly tests whether receiving A first affected the later B response?
choices: Score the same A→B videos without labels
Record A→B at twice the frame rate
activity.explanation: Reversing order creates the missing comparison. Blinding targets scoring expectations, and a faster recording leaves the same exposure order in place.

evidence.title: A study with only one sequence
evidence.context: The researchers suspect A changes the later response to B.

evidence.title: Treatment order and scoring
evidence.context: The same treatment durations are used in both sequences.

tip: Acclimation is adjustment time: give every group the same waiting period before measuring.

title: Compare the treatment effects
body: 1. Subtract control from treatment within each condition, then compare those effects.
2. For before-and-after studies, compare changes instead of final values.
3. To test a new temperature, slope, or population, repeat the matched comparison there. Include both control and treatment, not just one new group.

activity.prompt: Which condition has the larger treatment-minus-control effect?
activity.explanation: Low light gives 8−3 = 5; high light gives 11−9 = 2. A larger final treated value need not mean a larger treatment effect.

evidence.title: Treatment at two light levels
evidence.context: Use treatment minus its matched control.

evidence.title: Treatment at two temperatures
evidence.context: Separate matched groups are measured for the same time.

tip: Compare each treatment with its own control before comparing the two effects.

title: Check what the instrument can measure
body: 1. Accuracy: close to the known true value. Precision: repeated readings close together.
2. A shared offset needs calibration; averaging more biased readings keeps the bias.
3. Small differences need fine enough markings. Also check exactly what result and time the study records.

activity.prompt: A ruler marked only every 1 cm is used to compare lengths expected to differ by 0.2 cm. What is the most direct improvement?
choices: Read the same coarse mark more times
Use a ruler with finer graduations
Measure twice as many samples with the same coarse ruler
Use a calibrated ruler with the same 1 cm graduations
activity.explanation: Finer graduations directly improve resolution of the expected 0.2 cm difference. Repetition or more samples does not give an individual reading finer marks. Calibration addresses systematic accuracy, but a calibrated ruler with the same coarse graduations still has the stated resolution limit.

evidence.title: Measuring a small length difference
evidence.context: The study uses independent samples and the same measurement endpoint.

evidence.title: Checking a thermometer
evidence.context: The certified reference temperature is 50.0°C.

tip: Name exactly what is measured: dry sediment needs water removed; movement needs before-and-after positions.

title: Say only what the study shows
body: 1. Name the measured groups, result, and conditions.
2. A mean describes the group average, not every individual.
3. Do not extend one experiment to all species, places, or future conditions.

activity.prompt: Which conclusion stays within the study?
choices: Every treated seedling gained exactly 2 g
The treatment had the larger mean mass under the tested conditions
The treatment will have the same effect in every soil
activity.explanation: The means differ by 2 g in the stated experiment. Means do not give every individual result, and one soil/time combination does not establish every soil.

evidence.title: Seedling mass
evidence.context: One species, one soil, 10 days. Individual masses were not identical.

evidence.title: Panel output under one lamp
evidence.context: Six panels per group; individual changes vary. All panels use the same lamp.

tip: Keep the conclusion’s group, time, and conditions as narrow as the experiment.

title: Translate each scientist’s claim
body: 1. Write each claim as “if this cause changes, this result should follow.”
2. For “according to Scientist X,” use X’s claim even if the data disagree.
3. A prediction shared by both scientists cannot tell their explanations apart.

activity.prompt: F proposes trapped air; G proposes newly formed oxygen. Which observation alone is shared and therefore weak for separating them?
choices: Gas is mostly oxygen absent initially
Bubbling persists after dissolved air is removed
activity.explanation: Both mechanisms can produce visible bubbles. Their chemical source, not the presence of bubbles, is the disagreement.

evidence.title: Two sources of bubbles
evidence.context: Both accounts allow visible bubbles; they disagree about where the gas comes from.

rows: New oxygen from a light-driven reaction

evidence.title: Why is lake water cloudy?
evidence.context: The filter removes clay but leaves dissolved salt unchanged.

tip: Use a two-column scratch note: scientist name on one side, prediction on the other.

title: Test one proposed cause
body: 1. Find what each scientist says causes the result.
2. Compare a treatment that changes one proposed cause while keeping the other fixed.
3. Removing then restoring that cause can strengthen the link, but does not prove every detail.

activity.prompt: An inhibitor lowers light output, but also blocks oxygen supply. Why is a chemical-only conclusion uncertain?
choices: The chemical process must be the only cause because light output decreased
Oxygen supply changed along with the chemical process
The oxygen mechanism must be correct because oxygen delivery decreased
Repeating the same manipulation would separate the two mechanisms
activity.explanation: The manipulation changes both a chemical process and oxygen delivery, each relevant to a competing explanation. The fall in light output therefore cannot be assigned uniquely to either. Repeating that confounded manipulation does not separate them; a control preserving oxygen delivery while inhibiting the chemical would be more informative.

evidence.title: An inhibitor with two effects
evidence.context: One account requires a chemical process; the competing account requires oxygen delivery.

evidence.title: Removing and restoring clay
evidence.context: Salt, temperature, and lighting stay fixed.

tip: Check that removing one cause did not accidentally remove the competing cause too.

title: Possible does not mean proven
body: 1. Ask whether the evidence shows a process can happen or that it actually happened here.
2. A necessary condition must be met; meeting it alone does not prove the whole explanation.
3. Look for evidence specific to the event before choosing its cause.

activity.prompt: Rock fragments survive both river transport and glacier transport. What follows about a particular deposit?
activity.explanation: Survival demonstrates that either process could deliver fragments. Evidence about the particular deposit is still required to choose its actual history.

evidence.title: Rock transport trials
evidence.context: No route traces or historical observations from the deposit are supplied.

evidence.title: Spores survive two routes
evidence.context: The trials test survival during transport, not the valley’s actual history.

tip: “Could happen” answers possibility; “did happen here” requires evidence about this event.

title: Hold the competing cause still
body: 1. Choose the cause you want to test.
2. Find two rows where that cause changes and the competing cause stays the same.
3. Compare their results. A pattern can support a cause without showing its inner mechanism.

activity.prompt: To test a humidity-driven explanation against a light-driven one, which comparison isolates humidity?
activity.explanation: Hold light fixed and change humidity so that a response difference targets humidity. Changing both factors mixes the predictions.

evidence.title: Humidity or light?
evidence.context: Other conditions and measurement time are fixed. Pick the pair that tests humidity.

evidence.title: Salt or temperature?
evidence.context: Account A predicts a salt effect; B predicts a temperature effect on color score.

tip: Read across one fixed condition instead of comparing rows that change both factors.

title: Make the predictions disagree
body: 1. Write what each model predicts for the same test.
2. Pick a condition where the predictions differ.
3. A result that both models expect cannot choose between them, even if measured perfectly.

activity.prompt: Both models predict 6 at setting A but predict 9 and 15 at B. Which setting is more informative?
choices: Neither, because a model must match every setting before it can be tested
activity.explanation: At B the models make different predictions, 9 and 15, so an adequate measurement can distinguish them. Both predict 6 at A; measuring that shared prediction more precisely does not separate them. A model need not first be shown correct at all settings before an informative test is possible.

evidence.title: Two settings
evidence.context: Both settings are within both models’ stated ranges and can be measured well.

evidence.title: Which cue do organisms follow?
evidence.context: Heat is placed west and moisture east. All other conditions are matched.

tip: If both scientists predict the same result, that result cannot choose between them.

title: Check every part of a claim
body: 1. Split a prediction into its parts, then check each part against the data.
2. A match to one part does not rescue a failed part. A result without a required condition disproves that requirement.
3. For removal tests, compare each change with the same baseline. More than one cause can matter.

activity.prompt: A model claims germination needs both dry soil and warmth. Germination occurs in warm wet soil. Which claim is contradicted by this observation?
choices: Warmth and dry soil together are sufficient
activity.explanation: Germination in wet soil is a counterexample to dry soil being necessary. Warmth is present, so its necessity is not contradicted. A result under a different set of conditions also does not disprove that dry soil alone, or warm dry soil, could be sufficient; necessity and sufficiency are distinct claims.

evidence.title: A two-part germination claim
evidence.context: A model says both dry soil and warmth are required. Measurements are reliable.

evidence.title: Does growth need light and iron?
evidence.context: Model K says both sunlight and iron are required.

tip: For removal tests, subtract the untreated value from each result before comparing effects.

workedCases.label: Another case: check both trends
workedCases.text:
Question: A model predicts fewer fossils as the dryness indicator rises. Does the table agree?

1. Fossils fall from 30 to 12.
2. The dryness indicator rises from 2 to 6. Both predicted directions match.

Supported answer: Yes, both trends agree.

Watch for: Agreement supports this prediction; it does not prove a unique cause.

evidence.title: Two parts of one prediction
evidence.context: The same counting method was used in both layers.

workedCases.label: Another case: compare removal effects
workedCases.text:
Question: Which removed material has the larger measured effect on transmission?

1. Removing solids changes transmission by 35 − 10 = 25 points.
2. Removing droplets changes it by 20 − 10 = 10 points. Both changes matter.

Supported answer: Solids have the larger removal effect; both affect transmission.

Watch for: A larger effect does not make that material the only cause.

evidence.title: Matched removal tests
evidence.context: Only the named material was removed; everything else was kept the same.

title: Make a prediction from the rule
body: 1. A model may be an equation or a rule in words. Identify the requested input or condition.
2. Substitute into the whole equation, or apply the stated comparison. Keep units matched.
3. Compare prediction with observation at the same input. Do not accept a model just because its values rise.

activity.prompt: Model R predicts y = 4x+2. What is its prediction at x = 3?
activity.explanation: Substitute into the complete expression: 4×3+2 = 14. Omitting the intercept gives 12, which is a different model.

evidence.title: Model R
evidence.context: Use y = 4x + 2. Both variables are dimensionless.

evidence.title: Model G
evidence.context: G predicts y = 5t − 2, with time t in seconds and length y in cm.

tip: For a density rule, denser-than-liquid objects sink; less-dense objects rise. Compare densities first.

workedCases.label: Another case: compare every row
workedCases.text:
Question: Which model matches all three measurements?

1. At x = 1, both models give 2, so that row cannot separate them.
2. At x = 2 and 3, L gives 4 and 6; S gives 4 and 8. Only S matches every row.

Supported answer: S only.

Watch for: One matching row cannot prove a model. Keep substituting into the whole rule.

evidence.title: Two model rules
evidence.context: L predicts \(y = 2x\). S predicts \(y = 2^x\), so its output doubles each time x rises by 1.

workedCases.label: Another case: a rule in words
workedCases.text:
Question: Which object rises and which sinks?

1. Compare each object with the liquid, not with the other object.
2. 0.8 is below 1.2; 1.5 is above 1.2.

Supported answer: The ball rises; the bead sinks.

Watch for: Both are in the same liquid. The rule works without inventing an equation.

evidence.title: A verbal model
evidence.context: Ignoring flow and surface effects: an object less dense than the liquid rises; one denser sinks.

title: Add the same amount or multiply?
body: 1. Check whether each step adds a fixed amount or multiplies by a fixed factor.
2. Count the number of time intervals, not the number of labels.
3. Write the values in order. Halving and doubling apply to the previous amount.

activity.prompt: A substance retains one third each hour. Starting at 81 mg, how much remains after 3 h?
activity.explanation: Apply the factor three times: 81→27→9→3 mg. Subtracting 3 mg per hour would model a different process.

evidence.title: A shrinking substance
evidence.context: Each hour, one-third of the previous amount remains.

evidence.title: A tripling population
evidence.context: The population triples every 2 h while nutrients remain sufficient.

tip: Multiplying both group counts by the same factor keeps their shares of the total unchanged.

title: Test a model where it applies
body: 1. Find the model’s allowed range and conditions (its domain).
2. Calculate its prediction at a tested point inside that range.
3. A reliable mismatch there challenges the model. An outside point tests an extension it may never have claimed.

activity.prompt: A model applies at 10–30°C. Which observation tests its claim most directly?
choices: A result from a different material outside its scope
activity.explanation: Twenty-two degrees lies within the stated domain and holds the modeled material fixed. The other choices test an unsupported extension.

evidence.title: A temperature-limited model
evidence.context: The model applies at 10–30°C for one material. Other conditions match in the 22°C trial.

evidence.title: A limited model
evidence.context: The rule y = 4x applies to this material only for 1 ≤ x ≤ 6.

tip: An out-of-range result does not automatically disprove a model with a stated range.

title: Combine changes in a formula
body: 1. Handle one input change at a time.
2. A squared input squares its multiplier; a denominator divides the result.
3. Multiply the separate effects. Keep all unchanged quantities fixed.

activity.prompt: For R = kL/A, length doubles and area quadruples. What happens to resistance R?
activity.explanation: The length change gives ×2 and the area change gives ÷4. Together, 2/4 = 1/2, with k held constant.

evidence.title: A resistance rule
evidence.context: Use R = kL/A. Same material and temperature keep k fixed.

evidence.title: The rule u = ka²/b
evidence.context: k stays fixed throughout the changes.

tip: Multiplying a denominator makes the output smaller when the other inputs stay fixed.

title: Choose the best input to test
body: 1. Calculate both models at the same input.
2. Compare their predictions. A bigger measurable gap is easier to distinguish.
3. Keep the input inside both models’ ranges. Agreement at one input does not make the rules identical.

activity.prompt: Which input separates the predictions?
choices: Both give identical predictions at every x
activity.explanation: At x = 1 both give 5. At x = 2, A gives 7 and B gives 9, so that setting can separate them.

evidence.title: Different models
evidence.context: A: y = 2x + 3. B: y = 4x + 1. Both apply at the listed inputs; the instrument resolves 0.1 unit.

evidence.title: Two extension rules
evidence.context: L predicts x = 3F; M predicts x = F + 4. Both apply from 0 to 4 N.

tip: Calculate both predictions at the same input before choosing the most useful test.

title: Recognize a model’s upper limit
body: 1. A saturating model rises toward a limit instead of growing forever.
2. For q = 6C/(2+C), the fraction C/(2+C) is below 1 when C is positive.
3. So q stays below 6. An output reliably above that limit challenges the model.

activity.prompt: For q = 8C/(3+C), what value is approached as positive C becomes very large?
activity.explanation: Divide by C: q = 8/(3/C+1). The 3/C term approaches zero, so q approaches 8 from below.

evidence.title: Another saturating rule
evidence.context: Use q = 8C/(3+C) for positive C, including very large C.

evidence.title: A model that levels off
evidence.context: Use q = 6C/(2 + C) for positive C.

tip: A curve can keep increasing while getting closer and closer to a fixed ceiling.

title: Subtract the background first
body: 1. Raw reading = sample signal + background.
2. Subtract background from every reading before testing the sample’s pattern.
3. If asked for a future raw reading, predict the sample signal and add background back.

activity.prompt: Raw readings are 255 then 130 with constant background 5. What happens to the corrected signal?
activity.explanation: Subtract background from each reading: 255−5 = 250 and 130−5 = 125. The corrected signal halves. Halving the initial raw reading gives 127.5 rather than the observed corrected value; adding background gives 260 and 135; leaving both raw values unchanged omits the correction.

evidence.title: A different detector
evidence.context: Background stays at 5 counts/min.

evidence.title: Detector counts
evidence.context: Background stays at 10 counts/min. The sample signal halves each equal interval.

tip: Keep detector distance fixed: moving the sample can change counts without changing decay.

title: Use both sets of evidence
body: 1. Check the model’s conditions first, even if they are in a different graph.
2. Compare every relevant result with its prediction. One reliable mismatch needs explaining; another match does not erase it.
3. For a follow-up, change the proposed cause in matched control and treatment groups while keeping other conditions fixed.

activity.prompt: Model A fits Experiment 1 but contradicts reliable Experiment 2 under its own stated conditions. What is justified?
choices: Its first success is sufficient to retain the original claim unchanged
Its original stated claim remains valid if Experiment 2 is omitted from the fit
A model that fits Experiment 2 must automatically explain Experiment 1
The model needs revision despite its first success
activity.explanation: Both experiments are reliable and satisfy the stated conditions, so the second contradiction requires revision despite the first success. Omitting a contradictory in-scope test does not repair the claim. A competing model must also face both datasets; fitting one does not automatically establish a fit to the other.

evidence.title: Testing one claim twice
evidence.context: Both experiments meet the model’s stated conditions and use reliable measurements.

evidence.title: Does extra light always help?
evidence.context: Model A says more light always increases growth, provided living-cell density stays constant. Each treatment is measured for the same time. The graph checks the required density condition; the table gives growth.

tip: A model must survive the inconvenient row as well as the row that fits.

workedCases.label: Another case: count first, then test a cause
workedCases.text:
Question: How much smaller is the mixed total, and how could you test nutrient shortage?

1. Separate total = 500 + 400 = 900. Mixed total = 200 + 300 = 500; the difference is 400.
2. Add nutrients to matched separate AND mixed cultures, keeping the other conditions fixed.

Supported answer: 400 fewer cells/mL; compare matched low- and high-nutrient cultures.

Watch for: Changing nutrients only in the mixed culture would mix treatment with culture type.

evidence.title: Separate versus mixed cultures
evidence.context: Counts are final densities under the same starting conditions. Nutrient shortage is a proposed cause, not an established fact.

title: Read pH without reversing it
body: 1. Lower pH means more hydrogen ions: more acidic.
2. Each one-unit decrease multiplies hydrogen-ion concentration by 10.
3. Enzyme activity is a separate measurement. Read its table instead of assuming more acid means more activity.

activity.prompt: A solution changes from pH 5 to pH 6. What happens to hydrogen-ion concentration?
choices: It decreases by one concentration unit
activity.explanation: A one-unit rise in pH means one tenth the hydrogen-ion concentration. The logarithmic direction reverses the change in acidity.

evidence.title: A change in pH
evidence.context: Compare aqueous solutions at the same temperature.

evidence.title: Acidity and enzyme activity
evidence.context: Solutions are at the same temperature.

tip: Lower pH means higher hydrogen-ion concentration; check the direction before counting powers of ten.

title: Keep track of atoms and leftovers
body: 1. Use the reaction’s required ratio to see which ingredient runs out first.
2. Count products and leftover molecules separately.
3. Atoms and total mass stay conserved in a closed system. The number of molecules can change when atoms regroup.

activity.prompt: For N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, what forms from 2 N₂ and 9 H₂ molecules?
activity.explanation: Two N₂ use six H₂ and form four NH₃, leaving three H₂. Nitrogen is the limiting reactant.

evidence.title: Making ammonia
evidence.context: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. The limiting reactant reacts completely and no material is lost.

evidence.title: Making water
evidence.context: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. No material leaves the sealed vessel.

tip: Count atoms in the leftovers too; the reaction does not make them disappear.

title: Use voltage, current, and resistance
body: 1. Use the stated rule V = IR. To find current, use I = V/R.
2. For resistance, use R = V/I.
3. Series resistances add. At the same voltage, more resistance gives less current.

activity.prompt: At 9 V across a fixed 30 Ω resistor, what current follows?
activity.explanation: I = V/R = 9/30 = 0.30 A. The other operations reverse or multiply the quantities.

evidence.title: One resistor
evidence.context: The resistor obeys V = IR at unchanged temperature.

evidence.title: Adding a resistor in series
evidence.context: The resistors obey V = IR at unchanged temperature. A second identical resistor is added in series.

tip: At fixed voltage, doubling series resistance halves current; it does not double current.

title: Combine forces, then divide by mass
body: 1. Opposite forces subtract. Same-direction forces add.
2. Use the total (net) force in a = Fnet/m.
3. Zero net force means no acceleration. A moving object can keep moving at constant speed.

activity.prompt: What acceleration follows for the moving cart?
activity.explanation: Net force is 20−4 = 16 N forward. Divide by mass 4 kg to get 4 m/s². Using only the pull gives 5; friction alone does not give the net acceleration.

evidence.title: A different moving cart
evidence.context: Use Fnet = ma; the forces act in opposite directions.

evidence.title: Forces on a cart
evidence.context: Only the two shown horizontal forces act.

tip: Draw opposite arrows, subtract their forces, then divide by the mass.

title: Separate oxygen made from oxygen left
body: 1. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in light, making sugars and releasing oxygen; plants also respire, using oxygen in light and dark.
2. Net change = oxygen made − oxygen used.
3. If oxygen use is known and unchanged, add it back to the net gain to find total production.

activity.prompt: Leaves use 4 units of oxygen per hour and show a net gain of 9 in light. With unchanged respiration, what is gross production?
activity.explanation: Net production equals gross minus consumption. Add back the 4 consumed: gross = 9+4 = 13 units per hour.

evidence.title: Another leaf sample
evidence.context: Both measurements cover 1 h. Respiration stays unchanged.

evidence.title: Leaves in light and dark
evidence.context: Equal leaf samples are measured for 1 h. Assume respiration uses oxygen at the same rate in both conditions.

tip: A no-leaf control checks whether the same oxygen change happens without leaves.

title: Read a melting plateau
body: 1. A flat temperature during melting does not mean heating stopped: energy changes the phase.
2. Read plateau temperature and plateau duration separately.
3. Same mass and phase change need the same energy. Twice the net heating power takes half the time.

activity.prompt: A melting plateau lasts 10 min at the stated net power. With the same mass and twice that power, about how long should it last?
activity.explanation: The same phase change requires the same energy. Twice the energy per minute supplies it in half the time: 10/2 = 5 min. The melting temperature can remain unchanged while duration changes.

evidence.title: A different melting sample
evidence.context: The same mass fully melts, with comparable heat loss. The shown plateau lasts 10 min at the original net power.

evidence.title: Heating a solid
evidence.context: Constant power; heat loss is negligible. Melting starts at minute 3 and finishes at minute 9.

tip: A melting temperature alone does not identify the substance; different materials can share that property.

title: Find the chance of a trait
body: 1. Under complete dominance, one dominant allele shows its trait; the recessive trait needs two recessive alleles.
2. List the possible allele pairs. Genotype is the pair; phenotype is the visible trait.
3. Expected count = probability × total offspring. Actual counts can vary by chance.

activity.prompt: For Cc × Cc with C completely dominant, how many recessive-phenotype offspring are expected among 160?
activity.explanation: The combinations are CC, Cc, Cc, cc; only one of four is recessive. Expected count is 160×1/4 = 40, not a guarantee that a real sample equals 40.

evidence.title: Cross: Cc × Cc
evidence.context: C is completely dominant. Each parent passes either allele equally often on average; genotype does not affect survival.

evidence.title: Cross: Bb × bb
evidence.context: B is dominant. Each parent passes either of its alleles with equal chance.

tip: Write the allele pairs first; two different pairs can produce the same visible trait.

title: Most common is not always a majority
body: 1. The mode is the category with the largest count.
2. A majority needs more than half of all observations.
3. A group’s most common response does not mean every individual chose it.

activity.prompt: Which summary is accurate?
choices: West was a majority at 7 of 18
West was the mode, although fewer than half chose it
activity.explanation: Seven is the largest category count, but 7/18 is below one-half. The other directions retain 11 observations.

evidence.title: Another group
evidence.context: Each of 18 animals gives one response.

evidence.title: Animal directions
evidence.context: Each of 20 animals chooses one direction.

tip: Largest category means mode; more than half means majority. Check both separately.

title: Compare fractions, not just counts
body: 1. Divide marked items by all items scored in that same sample.
2. Convert both fractions to percentages if that makes comparison easier.
3. Unequal sample sizes can be compared. Counts alone do not tell you whether a difference is statistically reliable.

activity.prompt: Which sample has the larger marked proportion?
activity.explanation: K is 10/40 = 25%; L is 12/60 = 20%. Unequal sample sizes can be normalized, and the larger count need not give the larger fraction.

evidence.title: New samples
evidence.context: The same scoring rule is used in both samples.

evidence.title: Marked fossils
evidence.context: Both layers use the same definition of a mark.

tip: Give every numerator its own sample denominator before comparing percentages.

title: Use wave speed, frequency, and wavelength
body: 1. Frequency is cycles per second; wavelength is distance per cycle.
2. Use speed = frequency × wavelength. Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.
3. Keep speed fixed only when the passage says the medium and conditions stay the same.

activity.prompt: At a fixed speed of 21 m/s, what wavelength accompanies frequency 7 Hz?
activity.explanation: Wavelength = speed/frequency = 21/7 = 3 m. The cycle unit cancels; multiplying would compute the wrong quantity.

evidence.title: A new wave
evidence.context: The medium stays unchanged. Use v = fλ.

evidence.title: Waves in one medium
evidence.context: Wave speed stays at 24 m/s. Use v = fλ.

tip: Keep frequency, wavelength, and speed separate; a new medium can change speed.

title: Can the sensor see the predicted signal?
body: 1. Find the model’s required signal and the sensor’s detection limit.
2. If the required signal is below that limit, “not detected” cannot rule it out.
